children.text: A sanctuary in the forests of Corella, Bohol, where you can observe the Philippine tarsier — one of the world's smallest primates — in its natural habitat. Following a guide along a short forest trail, you can quietly meet tarsiers napping while clinging to tree branches.
The Philippine tarsier, commonly just called the "tarsier," is one of the world's smallest primates, about
long and weighing roughly 80–160g. Its hallmarks are a tail longer than its body (about

), slender fingers tipped with round adhesive pads, and enormous eyes that take up half its face — each eyeball is said to be larger than its brain. Because the eyes are fixed in their sockets and cannot roll, the tarsier turns its head nearly 180 degrees to each side, and its bat-like ears swivel independently toward sounds. It sleeps by day in tangles of vines and bamboo thickets and hunts crickets, grasshoppers and small lizards after dark, and it can leap

at a time between trees. Endemic to the south-eastern islands of the Philippines such as Bohol, Samar, Leyte and Mindanao, it is classified as Near Threatened (NT) by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

The best-known place to meet tarsiers on Bohol is the sanctuary of the Philippine Tarsier Foundation (PTFI) on the forested slopes of Canapnapan village in Corella. The foundation was formed by local Bohol businessmen and registered in
, and the following year, on

, President Ramos issued Proclamation No. 1030 declaring the tarsier a specially protected wildlife species. Carlito Pizarras, a local who had caught tarsiers since childhood to hand over to his taxidermist father, turned to raising and protecting them, and has worked as the foundation's field supervisor since
; he is widely known as the "Tarsier Man." The genus name of the Philippine tarsier, "Carlito," comes from his name.
The forest managed by the foundation is only part of roughly
134 hectares

of public forest between Corella and Sikatuna, and the sanctuary that visitors actually enter is much smaller, at about 8 hectares. Guided by a ranger, visitors walk into a forest called the "sleeping area." It is an open forest with no roof, enclosed only by netting to keep out predators such as cats, so the foundation explains that tarsiers can climb out over the fence and go hunting at night. About 100 tarsiers live in the netted area, and roughly 1,000 are estimated to live in the surrounding protected forest. Guides check the sleeping branches every morning and point them out, so you can usually see three or four tarsiers, but because they are wild animals, a particular number is never guaranteed.
A visit begins at the visitor center by the entrance, followed by a walk along the forest trail with a guide, and it is over in
30 minutes–1 hour
. Children and older visitors can manage it at a slow pace, though parts of the trail are uphill and slippery after rain. On
September 18, 2026

the foundation held an opening ceremony for its new tourism center and research center, and visitors are reportedly able to tour the research center and the tarsier viewing area with a guide, so please check the latest information before you go. Along with the Chocolate Hills and the Loboc River, it is a staple stop on Bohol countryside tours, and if animal welfare matters to you, this foundation-run sanctuary is a better choice than the private roadside facilities around Loboc and Bilar.
A guide is included with your entrance ticket. The guide points out the sleeping spots checked earlier that morning, and you usually meet three or four tarsiers one after another within
20–30 minutes
. The foundation asks that you spend no more than about five minutes in front of any one tarsier.

The visitor center at the entrance displays panels introducing tarsier ecology, breeding and conservation work, along with a real tarsier skeleton specimen. Looking around before you enter the forest makes the observation much more interesting.

blocks.title: Look at the eyes, ears and fingers

children.text: Each eyeball is larger than the brain and cannot move, so the tarsier turns its whole head to look around. Its big ears swivel independently toward sounds, and it grips branches with the round pads on its fingertips. If its ears twitch even while it sleeps, that is a sign the noise is bothering it, so lower your voice further.
The rule is to turn off the flash and the shutter sound and shoot from a step or two away. A smartphone's 2–3x zoom or portrait mode is enough for sharp photos, and drones are prohibited.

Ask your guide about how a hunter's son became a protector, why tarsiers do not thrive in captivity, and why their numbers rise slowly — a female bears only one young a year after a gestation of about six months.
The foundation says that all entrance fees and souvenir proceeds go toward conservation. Souvenirs bought at the foundation's shop are the ones whose proceeds go directly to that cause.

blocks.title: Blood Compact monument and Baclayon Church

children.text: Along the coastal road east of Tagbilaran stands a monument commemorating the blood compact sealed in
between the Spanish explorer Legazpi and the Bohol chieftain Sikatuna, and just beyond it is
Baclayon Church
, a coral-stone church completed in
. The church lost its bell tower in the 2013 earthquake and reopened after restoration in February 2018. You can see both in about
30 minutes
each, which makes them easy to fit in before or after the tarsiers.
Corella lies on the way to the
Loboc River
and the
Chocolate Hills
, so it fits well early in a day tour.
Arrive at the Corella sanctuary when it opens, buy your ticket in cash, and take in the visitor center exhibits and briefing.
Walk the forest trail with a guide, observe three or four sleeping tarsiers, and take photos. The forest trail takes about
20–30 minutes
Rest at the souvenir shop and snack stall, and look around the research center and the new tourism center exhibits.
Head toward the Loboc River lunch cruise pier. It takes
30–40 minutes
by car.

Look around Baclayon Church and its museum.

Enjoy the floating buffet lunch cruise on the Loboc River, then return to Tagbilaran.

1 hour
Enter as the Corella sanctuary opens and walk the forest trail.
Board the Loboc River lunch cruise. Many packages include a buffet and live music.

Climb to the Chocolate Hills viewpoint and look down on the cone-shaped hills. If you have energy left, try the ATV.
Return to Panglao by car.
The flight from Manila to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG) takes about
1 hour–1 hour 20 minutes
, with Philippine Airlines group flights and Cebu Pacific operating several flights a day. One-way fares from Manila start from about
on cheap days and rise sharply in peak season. Direct flights from Incheon to Bohol operate seasonally, so check before booking.
The airport is on Panglao Island, about
20km
from Tagbilaran, and the drive to the Corella sanctuary takes
40 minutes–1 hour 10 minutes
. A taxi or private car costs about
one way, a private van seating 5 to 10 people about
, and a shared van about
per person. There is no public transport straight from the airport to the sanctuary, so you must go through Tagbilaran.

2 hours

Tagbilaran port is in the Booy district, about
2km
from the city center, and from the port to the Corella sanctuary is about
14km
, or
20–30 minutes
by car. Boats are canceled when seas are rough or a typhoon approaches, so reconfirm your sailing the day before.
Take a jeepney or bus bound for Corella from the Dao Integrated Bus Terminal in Tagbilaran. The fare is about
and the ride takes
30–40 minutes
. Service is irregular, so set out early, and say clearly "Corella, Tarsier Sanctuary" so you are not confused with facilities near Loboc. From Corella town to the sanctuary entrance is about
3–4km
uphill, so most people take a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) for about
and
10 minutes
Hiring a tricycle or habal-habal from Tagbilaran city for a round trip, including waiting time, costs about
Most travelers visit on a countryside tour vehicle (about
per vehicle from Panglao). From Panglao to Corella is about
, or
1 hour
by car, and a scooter can be rented for about

a day, but because of the uphill stretches and sharp curves, only experienced riders should do so. Depending on the tour package, drivers sometimes take you to other tarsier facilities near Loboc and Bilar rather than Corella, so tell your driver clearly which place you want in advance.
Tarsiers sleep through the day all year, so they can be seen in any season. Bohol's temperatures stay mostly within
all year, and the dry season from
December–May
, when forest trails dry out and skies are clear, is the most pleasant. Within it,
March–May
is the driest but midday heat is intense and you will sweat a lot on the uphill forest trail. In the rainy season from
June–October
rain is frequent, the trail is slippery, mosquitoes increase, and heavy rain can suspend visits. Rain can fall in any month on Bohol, and showers are frequent even from
November–January
, so it is wise to bring a raincoat even in the dry season.
The foundation's official opening hours are from
to
, though some travel sites list
9 AM–4 PM

, so avoid late-afternoon visits. Because tarsiers sleep all day, the time of day makes little difference to what you see; what matters more is how crowded it is. The foundation recommends the afternoon because tour groups crowd in during the morning, while individual travelers' reviews recommend a weekday right after opening. Right after opening or after lunch, between
1 PM–2 PM
, is relatively quiet.
Bohol sits on the southern edge of the typhoon track, so it is hit directly less often than Luzon, but not never.
December 2021
saw Typhoon Odette (international name Rai) strike Bohol directly and cause major damage. Typhoon and low-pressure risk rises from
October
through
January
, so in that period check the Philippine weather bureau (PAGASA) forecast and allow for the possibility that boats between Cebu and Tagbilaran are canceled.

children.text: Fares are rough estimates as of
and may vary with local conditions.
There is almost no lodging near the sanctuary, so most visitors stay in
Alona Beach
on
Panglao Island
or in Tagbilaran city and visit for the day. Resorts at Alona Beach run
or more per night, and hotels in Tagbilaran city about
. If you want a quiet stay in nature, you can also sleep in a bungalow on the Loboc River and visit the sanctuary early in the morning.

The sanctuary entrance has only a stall selling drinks and simple snacks. For meals, use the buffet on the Loboc River lunch cruise or a restaurant in Tagbilaran. Tagbilaran has plenty of food courts in long-established malls (such as Island City Mall) and local seafood restaurants, handy before or after the tour. Bohol's signature treats are calamay, a chewy glutinous-rice sweet sold in coconut shells (the version from Jagna in the south is famous), broas (ladyfinger biscuits) from Baclayon, and peanut kisses, made from peanuts. Peanut kisses are cheap at the Tagbilaran public market and are also sold at the airport and the pier.
There are no ATMs near the sanctuary. Bring your entrance fee and souvenir money in small bills of cash.
The foundation says no advance booking is needed, but groups and school visits are best arranged in advance. Check the latest fees and hours on the
foundation's official website (tarsierfoundation.com)
On the trail, walk in single file and keep your voice down. It helps to explain to children beforehand why they need to be quiet.
Tarsiers sit in shady spots among the branches, so photos tend to come out dark. Turn off night mode and raise the exposure slightly, but never use a flash.
Bring long pants, mild-scented insect repellent, a thin raincoat and a towel to wipe off sweat. After rain the soil is slippery, so shoes with soles are better than sandals.
A countryside tour driver may take you to another roadside facility, saying it is cheaper. If animal welfare matters to you, ask for the foundation's sanctuary in Corella.
Hours are generally
, and it is safest to assume the last entry is around
3 PM
. If you make it the last stop on a tour you can easily miss the entry cutoff, so visit in the morning or early afternoon.

Tarsiers are extremely sensitive to noise, light and touch, and the foundation explains that heavy stress can harm their health and even kill them. Never touch them or fire a flash, and do not make loud noises.
Feeding tarsiers, shaking branches and touching them are all prohibited, and only guides may approach a tarsier. Poking a selfie stick close to take a picture is also not allowed.

Private facilities such as the roadside "tarsier conservation areas" near Loboc and Bilar are not run by the foundation. They are criticized for keeping animals on branches close to people during the day, so even though the fee (about ₱80) is cheaper, do not confuse them with the Corella sanctuary.
The tarsier is a species protected under Proclamation No. 1030. If you see a place where people buy and sell them or keep them as pets, do not patronize it and report it to the Department of Tourism.
Fees and hours differ from one source to another. The foundation says ₱150, reviews list ₱60–170, and opening is split between
and
9 AM
. They may change after the new center's opening, so check the latest announcement before you go.
The trail has uphill and narrow stretches and turns to mud in the rain, so have children hold your hand as they walk.
